title: William Carey
hook: a poor shoemaker who taught himself languages sails to India: expect great things, attempt great things

segments.voice: Yesterday, the block close and its line from Lamentations: both reformed, both failed, both produced saints. Your line was reformed and reforming. What kind and true thing did you say about another church or group? Day nine hundred sixteen.

A new block begins today: the modern church across the world. It starts at a cobbler's bench in an English village. A young shoemaker sits mending boots, and propped up in front of him, the story goes, is a book in Latin or Greek, open while he works. On the wall hangs a homemade map of the world, with notes about the peoples of each land. He is poor. He has no university degree. He has taught himself to read languages his neighbors have never seen. And he has a question the older ministers would rather not hear. Today: William Carey.
screen: `A BOOK PROPPED ON THE COBBLER'S BENCH.`

segments.voice: His question was simple. Jesus told his disciples to go into all the world. Did that still apply to ordinary Christians, or was it only for the apostles? Carey, a Baptist preacher by now as well as a shoemaker, thought it still applied. A story is told that when he raised it at a meeting of ministers, an older man told him to sit down: if God wanted to reach the nations, God would do it without him. Carey didn't sit down for long. He wrote a pamphlet arguing his case, and then he preached a sermon on a verse from Isaiah: "Enlarge the place of thy tent, and let them stretch forth the curtains of thine habitations: spare not, lengthen thy cords, and strengthen thy stakes". Make the tent bigger. Out of that sermon, people remember a motto in two halves: expect great things from God, attempt great things for God. Notice the order. Expect comes first: the great things are looked for from God before they are attempted for God. Not long after, a missionary society was formed, and Carey sailed for India with his family. It was hard. Money ran short, there was illness and grief at home, and fruit came slowly. He worked, studied, and with colleagues set up a press and a college, and spent his life translating the Bible into languages of India, including Bengali. Indian scholars and Christians worked alongside him. And later readers have asked hard questions about how missions traveled with empire. That's tomorrow's story. Today's is a shoemaker who looked at a map and refused to make his tent smaller.

Here's the practice: attempt one big thing, starting small. Sit up, and let your feet rest flat on the floor. Picture your own tent: the size of your life right now. Is there one thing you've stopped hoping for because it seemed too big? A course, a reconciliation, a book, a move, a gift you'd love to give. Name it. Don't plan the whole thing. Just let yourself expect it for a minute. If you pray, you can bring it to God. If you don't, just hold it in your mind. The bell holds the time.
William Carey. An English shoemaker and Baptist preacher who taught himself languages, preached on enlarging the tent, sailed to India, and spent his life translating the Bible there.
Your line: expect great things. Today, take the very first step on that big thing: one call, one page, one form, one honest conversation. Day nine hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Baptists and other Protestants remember Carey as a pioneer of the modern missionary movement, and churches in India remember the translation work of Carey and his Indian colleagues.

notes: Claims rule: no dates, ages or counts given (no number of languages or years).
The motto 'expect great things from God, attempt great things for God' is given as what people remember; the earliest wording may have been 'Expect great things. Attempt great things.' Confirm.
The 'sit down, young man' anecdote (John Ryland Sr.) is framed as 'a story is told'; it is disputed.
Book propped on the bench and the homemade map are framed as 'the story goes'; confirm.
'Indian Christians and scholars worked alongside him' (pundits such as Mrityunjay Vidyalankar, colleagues Marshman and Ward, the Serampore press and college); confirm wording.
